intro: This question helps us find the best place for you to begin.

widget.instructions: Drag the endpoints, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Enter or Space switches between included and not included. Typing in the answer box moves the line too.

stem: Write the set {x ∈ ℝ : {{cond}}} as an interval.

hints.text: Mark the endpoints on the number line. Is each endpoint included or not?
Use [ or ] when the endpoint is included (≤ or ≥) and ( or ) when it is not (< or >). Watch the test point: it lights up exactly where the condition holds.
∞ is never included, so it always takes a round bracket.

open-closed-confusion.text: The endpoints are right, but check which ones are included. ≤ and ≥ include the endpoint (square bracket, filled dot); < and > don't (round bracket, hollow dot). The ringed endpoint is the one to fix.

infinity-closed.text: ∞ is not a number you can reach, so it can never be included. Use a round bracket next to it.

wrong-endpoints.text: Check the endpoints against the inequality. Each endpoint should be one of the numbers in the condition, or ±∞.

missing-piece.text: This set is a single interval. Check your endpoints.

extra-piece.text: This set is a single interval, without gaps.

generic.text: Mark the endpoints first, then decide on each bracket.

workedSolution.text: Endpoints: {{loText}} ({{loState}}) and {{hiText}} ({{hiState}}). Watch the test point: it is in the set exactly where the condition holds.

open-closed-confusion.front: Which bracket goes with ≤ and which with <?
open-closed-confusion.back: ≤ or ≥ → square bracket [ ]; < or > → round bracket ( ).

wrong-endpoints.front: Where do an interval's endpoints come from?
wrong-endpoints.back: From the numbers in the inequality, or ±∞ when one side is unbounded.

generic.front: Convert a < x ≤ b to interval notation.
